finding.claim: Broken authorization: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of calling require_edit(), so any authenticated user can overwrite the body of any document they neither own nor edit.
finding.source: Any authenticated user (g.user) sending PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...} for an arbitrary doc_id
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] (docs.py:20), modifying a protected document

trace.note: doc = DOCS[doc_id] fetched with no ownership check
can_edit(g.user, doc) return value ignored, so no abort(403)

finding.guards_checked: Compared with update_title (docs.py:27), which correctly uses require_edit and aborts 403. No other auth decorator or before_request hook exists in the file. g.user is never set in this file, so authentication is assumed to be handled elsewhere, but it does not matter because the authorization check is a no-op. Missing doc_id raises KeyError (500) rather than 404, which is a minor robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: can_edit() (docs.py:8) returns a bool and is called as a bare statement at docs.py:19, so its result is discarded; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) is the aborting variant but is only used in update_title (docs.py:27). No decorator or before_request hook exists.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) and discards the boolean, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any authenticated user without the abort(403) that require_edit would raise (docs.py:13).
